questions.q: How many times does a Salesforce trigger fire for a single DML operation that affects 200 records?
options: 200 times, once per record
It depends on whether the records were inserted via the UI or the API
Once, with Trigger.new holding the full collection of all 200 records
Twice — once for validation and once for the actual save
questions.explain: A trigger fires once per transaction regardless of batch size, with Trigger.new holding the entire collection of records being processed together.

questions.q: Why does a trigger with SOQL or DML inside a per-record loop often pass every manual test but fail in production?
options: Because manual UI testing almost always saves one record at a time, so the loop never actually executes more than once until a real bulk operation (Data Loader, bulk API, a mass Flow update) sends many records through it at once
Because the Developer Console silently raises governor limits during testing
Because triggers are disabled by default in sandboxes
Because SOQL queries behave differently in production than in a sandbox
questions.explain: A single-record save only ever runs the loop body once, so the per-record query or DML call never multiplies — the bug is invisible until a genuinely bulk operation sends many records through the same trigger invocation at once.

questions.q: In the bulkified AccountTrigger example, how many total SOQL queries are issued regardless of whether Trigger.new holds 1 record or 200?
options: One query per Account, same as the non-bulkified version
Zero, because bulkification eliminates the need for any query
It depends on how many Contacts exist, not how many Accounts are in the trigger
Exactly one — the query runs once against the whole collected set of IDs, not once per Account
questions.explain: The entire point of bulkification is a flat cost: collecting IDs into a Set and querying once outside the loop means exactly one SOQL query runs no matter how many records are in the batch.

questions.q: What is the tell-tale sign that a helper method (not a trigger directly) is written in a bulk-safe way?
options: It uses only local variables and no SOQL at all
Its signature accepts a collection (like List<Account>), and any query or DML inside it happens once per call, not once per element of that list
It is marked with the @future annotation
It always returns a Boolean indicating success or failure
questions.explain: A bulk-safe method is designed around processing a whole batch: it takes a collection as its parameter, and its governor-limit-consuming work (queries, DML) runs once per invocation rather than once per item in that collection.

questions.q: In the original non-bulkified AccountTrigger example, which two governor limits would be at the most direct and immediate risk if 150+ Accounts, each with multiple Contacts, were updated in one transaction?
options: Maximum heap size and maximum callout timeout
Total number of email invocations and total number of future calls
Total SOQL queries issued (100 synchronous) and total DML statements issued (150)
There is no risk, since Apex automatically converts loop-based DML into bulk DML
questions.explain: One SOQL query per Account quickly approaches the 100-query synchronous ceiling, and one update DML statement per Contact (nested inside the Account loop) quickly approaches the 150-DML-statement ceiling — exactly the two limits this lesson's governor-limits recap (Lesson 2) covered.
